To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) Norwegian citizens’ attitudes towards immigrants are largely driven by economic and cultural threat, and (2) Norwegian citizens’ policy preferences are largely driven by symbolic politics, with economic and cultural threat playing a comparatively small role.
Norwegian attitudes toward immigration policies are more influenced by symbolic politics while attitudes toward immigrants themselves are more influenced by group threat.

(1) economic and cultural threat are important factors in the formation of Norwegians’ attitudes toward immigrants; (2) the role of threat factors is stronger in attitudes toward immigrants than in attitudes toward voting rights for the non-citizen population; (3) symbolic politics are more important for attitudes toward voting rights than for attitudes toward immigrants; and (4) symbolic politics are also more important for attitudes of individuals with low political interest and knowledge than for those with high political interest and knowledge.

the formation of public opinion regarding immigration and immigration policy in Norway, and it is one of the first studies of its kind in the Scandinavian context.
